pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers, with the unknown in any position (8 + ? = 11; 5 = □ − 3; 6 + 6 = □). Ages 6–7, a procedural target resting on the meaning of '=' and the inverse relationship.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 'solve one-step problems... including missing number problems such as 7 = □ − 9' and Y2 'solve problems with addition and subtraction... and missing number problems'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.8 'Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers. For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of 8 + ? = 11, 5 = □ − 3, 6 + 6 = □.'
• Operational details: vary the unknown's POSITION deliberately (result unknown, change unknown, start unknown, answer-on-left) so the child cannot rely on 'add the two numbers I see'. Solve by choosing the inverse move and reading '=' as balance, not by keyword. Bar/part-whole models externalise which quantity is missing.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — solves 6 + 6 = □ and 8 + ? = 11. Tier B (age 7) — solves answer-left and subtraction-position forms (5 = □ − 3) correctly. Tier C (age 7+) — chooses the inverse operation for the unknown position and checks the answer by substituting back.
bestPractices: Systematically vary the unknown position (a+b=□, a+□=c, □+b=c, and answer-left forms) so pupils build a flexible method, not a keyword habit.
Represent each equation on a bar / part-whole model first to see which quantity is unknown before calculating.
Insist on substituting the answer back to check the equation balances.
Use non-standard forms (5 = □ − 3) early to defeat the left-to-right 'answer-comes-next' reading.
keyRepresentations: Bar model / part-whole diagram with the unknown segment shaded
Pan balance with an unknown mass on one side
Empty number line for count-on / inverse jumps
Fact-family triangle to pick the needed operation
Equation cards with the box in varied positions
commonMisconceptions: Adding the two visible numbers regardless of the box's position (8 + ? = 11 → 19).
Reading answer-left forms as backwards (5 = □ − 3 → writes 2, i.e. 5 − 3).
Always subtracting or always adding by keyword rather than by the unknown's role.
Not checking the solution by putting it back into the equation.
Treating '=' as 'work out the total' so a box before '=' is confusing.

learn.summary: Help 6–7 year olds find the unknown whole number in addition/subtraction equations where the unknown appears in any position (8 + ? = 11; 5 = □ − 3; 6 + 6 = □). The target is a flexible method built on reading '=' as 'both sides balance' and choosing the inverse move, not an 'add the two numbers I can see' habit. Vary the unknown's position deliberately (result, change, start, answer-on-left) and insist on checking by substituting the answer back.

activities.title: Balance the unknown with counters
feedback: If the child writes 2 for 5 = □ − 3: show that □ − 3 must equal 5, so starting from 5 we add back the 3 that was taken away, giving □ = 8 (5 + 3 = 8). Try more answer-left forms.
If the child adds the two visible numbers (8 + ? = 11 → 19): point to the bar — 11 is the whole, 8 is one part, the box is the missing part, found by 11 − 8 = 3.
Live true/false balance feedback as counters are added lets the child self-correct before stating an answer.
Praise explicitly when the child checks by substituting back, e.g. 'you put 3 back and 8 + 3 does make 11'.
activities.rationale: A missing-number target is procedural and benefits from repeated practice with immediate feedback across varied positions. A balance or part-whole representation externalises which quantity is missing and makes '=' mean balance rather than 'compute the total', which is intended to address the answer-left misread. Note that a physical two-pan balance shows addition most naturally; the subtraction form 5 = □ − 3 is modelled by filling the box and removing 3, an approximation of the equation. Optional interactions such as a slider, draggable counters, or a live beam that tips make the balancing mechanism concrete; they are helpful examples, not required.
sourceClaims: Varying the position of the unknown (result/change/start unknown) changes problem difficulty, and children commonly add the two visible numbers regardless of position.
1.OA.8 requires determining the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation, with the examples 8 + ? = 11, 5 = □ − 3, 6 + 6 = □.
learnerActions: Set out an equation with a box, e.g. 5 = □ − 3, on a two-pan balance or bar model where one side already shows 5.
Add or remove counters in the box until both sides match: too few and the box side is too light, too many and it tips down.
State the value that makes both sides balance (for 5 = □ − 3 the box must hold 8, because □ − 3 has to equal 5).
Repeat with the unknown in every position: 8 + ? = 11, □ + 6 = 12, 6 + 6 = □.
Check each solved equation by putting the found number back in and confirming both sides match.
activities.intendedInsight: The box holds whatever value makes the two sides equal; '=' means balance, so an answer-on-left form like 5 = □ − 3 is not 'backwards' — it is the same balancing task. One balancing method works for every position.

activities.title: Solve by the inverse, then check
feedback: If the child only guesses and checks repeatedly: prompt the inverse move via the fact family — 'the whole is 11, one part is 8, so the missing part is 11 − 8' — to build efficiency. The concept need not be re-taught here.
If the wrong operation is chosen, return to a bar model to re-identify which quantity is unknown before computing.
Reinforce that the check (substituting back) is part of the method, not an optional extra.
activities.rationale: Choosing the inverse for the unknown's position is the efficient method the standard targets; a fact-family representation helps pupils map position to operation. Trial-and-error can give correct answers but does not build the intended fluency, so prompting the inverse addresses a genuine performance gap.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.8 requires determining the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation, with the examples 8 + ? = 11, 5 = □ − 3, 6 + 6 = □.
Y1–Y2 pupils solve missing-number problems such as 7 = □ − 9 and problems with addition and subtraction.
learnerActions: Given □ + 9 = 14, convert it to the inverse: 14 − 9, and compute □ = 5.
Given 8 + ? = 11, use 11 − 8 = 3 rather than guessing and testing values.
Use a fact-family triangle (whole 14; parts 9 and 5) to pick the operation needed for the unknown's position.
Substitute the answer back and confirm the sentence is true.
Practise a mixed set covering result-unknown, change-unknown, start-unknown and answer-left forms.
activities.intendedInsight: Once you know which quantity is the whole and which is a part, you can go straight to the answer with the inverse operation instead of slow trial-and-error.

activities.title: Explain your move (strategy talk)
feedback: If the child says they 'added the two numbers', probe where the box sits and what '=' requires, then re-model on a bar.
Note that for 5 = □ − 3 and □ − 3 = 5 the answer is the same (□ = 8), because both say the box minus 3 equals 5; discuss why.
Accept any correct reasoning the child can justify; press for the inverse when they rely only on guessing.
activities.rationale: Discussion is a supporting diagnostic that reveals strategy, not just answers; it may complement rather than replace hands-on practice with feedback. It is especially useful for catching the left-to-right 'answer-comes-next' reading, though talk alone does not provide the repeated solving practice a procedural target needs.
sourceClaims: Varying the position of the unknown (result/change/start unknown) changes problem difficulty, and children commonly add the two visible numbers regardless of position.
learnerActions: Solve a varied-position equation aloud, e.g. 5 = □ − 3, then explain how you decided what to do.
Answer probes: 'Which of these could you check with an addition, and how?' and 'What if it were □ − 3 = 5 instead of 5 = □ − 3 — would the answer change?'
Show how you'd check that your answer to 8 + ? = 11 makes the sentence true.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the reasoning surfaces whether a child is using a keyword/positional habit or genuinely reasoning from which quantity is missing.

activities.title: Anchor each position to an operation (worked bar models)
feedback: Use the diagram to correct an added-the-two-numbers error by showing the box is a part, not the whole.
A fixed worked example can anchor the mapping, but pupils still need to then solve fresh items themselves to build fluency.
activities.rationale: A static annotated bar model is a useful anchor for connecting position to operation. On its own it does not provide practice with feedback, so pair it with solving fresh items; it is a scaffold toward the balancing/inverse practice rather than a substitute for it.
learnerActions: Study a worked part-whole/bar diagram for each unknown position (result, change, start, answer-left) with the missing segment highlighted.
Reveal, for each, which operation finds the missing part and why (whole − part = part; part + part = whole).
Then solve matching fresh equations and verify by substitution.
activities.intendedInsight: Each position maps to a specific inverse move once you identify the whole and the parts; the diagram makes that mapping visible.

constraints: Systematically vary the unknown's position (a+b=□, a+□=c, □+b=c, and answer-left forms) so pupils build a flexible method, not a keyword habit.
Introduce non-standard forms (5 = □ − 3) early to counter the left-to-right 'answer-comes-next' reading.
Read '=' as 'both sides balance', not 'work out the total'; a box before '=' is legitimate.
Insist on checking by substituting the found value back into the equation.

Fill-in-the-blank and multiple-choice practice (e.g. choosing the inverse calculation that solves □ + 9 = 14, with '2' as a wrong option for 5 = □ − 3) is useful for spaced retrieval and checking fluency, but recognition/selection does not itself require the child to construct and reason through the balancing move, so pair it with constructed solving.
Worked static diagrams anchor the position→operation mapping but do not themselves provide practice with feedback; follow them with fresh items to solve.
Trial-and-error can produce correct answers but does not build the intended inverse-method fluency; prompt the inverse once accuracy is secure.
Keep the wrong-answer value '2' (from 5 − 3) only as an incorrect option; the correct answer to 5 = □ − 3 is 8.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels a numeric/non-spatial '3D adds nothing' claim; this comparative-necessity claim is not established by the cited sources and has been dropped rather than asserted. A 2D balance/bar is proposed on its affordances (making balance and the missing part visible), not as the uniquely necessary medium.

Self-audit of arithmetic and logic: 8 + ? = 11 → 3; 5 = □ − 3 → 8 (box minus 3 equals 5, so box = 5 + 3 = 8); 6 + 6 = □ → 12; □ + 9 = 14 → 5; □ + 6 = 12 → 6. The answer-left value '2' (from 5 − 3) is the misconception value and must only appear as a wrong option, never as a correct answer.

Representational caveat: a two-pan balance models addition most directly; the subtraction form 5 = □ − 3 is handled by filling the box and removing 3, which approximates the equation rather than weighing it literally. This is stated in Activity 1 so the scaffold's limit is visible to the teacher.
Noted and preserved the clarification that 5 = □ − 3 and □ − 3 = 5 have the same solution (□ = 8); the source probe asks pupils to consider this.

The standards claims (DfE; CCSS 1.OA.8) attached to Activities 1–2 ground the objective (determining the unknown across positions); they do not empirically establish that the inverse method or the balance representation is more effective than alternatives. Efficacy wording is kept as intended/proposed.

Source 'verified' flags are mixed (DfE true; CCSS and Cognitively Guided Instruction false in the row); confidence was legacy 'high'. No fresh verification performed, so no confidence upgrade is claimed.

probeDeeper: How did you decide what to do for 5 = □ − 3?
Which of these three could you check using an addition, and how?
What if it were □ − 3 = 5 instead of 5 = □ − 3 — would the answer change?
Show me how you'd check that your answer to 8 + ? = 11 makes the sentence true.
assess.correctAnswer: ? = 3; □ = 8; □ = 12. Watch for the child using the inverse (11 − 8 = 3; 5 + 3 = 8) on the first two and adding directly on the last, and for correct handling of the answer-left/subtraction-position form.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the two visible numbers regardless of the box's position — 8 + ? = 11 becomes 8 + 11 = 19 in the box.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model on a bar: 11 is the whole, 8 a part; the box is the missing part, found by 11 − 8. Re-establish what '=' constrains.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 19 (or otherwise combines the two shown numbers) for a change-unknown item.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the answer-left form as backwards — 5 = □ − 3 solved as 5 − 3 = 2.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Balance model: □ − 3 must weigh the same as 5, so □ = 8; practise more answer-left forms.

errorPatterns.pattern: Solves only by slow trial-and-error / counting, never using the inverse to go straight to the answer.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — prompt the inverse move via the fact-family triangle; build efficiency.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Guesses values and checks repeatedly rather than computing 11 − 8 directly.

responseLevels.gap: Combines the two given numbers regardless of the box's position (e.g. 19, 2); standard result-unknown may be right by habit only.
responseLevels.full: Solves all three fluently, selecting the inverse operation for the unknown's position and verifying by substituting the answer back into the equation.
responseLevels.partial: Solves result-unknown and change-unknown forms but stumbles on the answer-left/subtraction-position item, or solves all only by slow trial-and-error without using the inverse.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these three and write the missing number in each box, working at the table while I watch: 8 + ? = 11; 5 = □ − 3; 6 + 6 = □.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three items place the unknown differently — change-unknown, start-of-a-subtraction with the answer on the left, and result-unknown. A child running an 'add the two numbers I can see' habit produces tell-tale wrong values (19 for the first, 2 for the second) while getting the standard third right. Watching HOW they solve, not just the answers, separates a flexible inverse method from a keyword habit.
